A_target.statement:
Let $R$ be a [[Definition:Noetherian Ring|Noetherian ring]].
Let $\map P I$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|property]] of [[Definition:Ideal of Ring|ideals]] of $R$ such that, for every ideal $I$, if $\map P J$ holds for every ideal $J \supsetneq I$, then $\map P I$ holds.
Then $\map P I$ holds for every ideal $I$ of $R$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\prec$ be a [[Definition:Well-Founded Relation|well-founded relation]] on a set $S$.
Then every non-empty subset of $S$ has a $\prec$-[[Definition:Minimal Element|minimal element]], and properties may be proved by considering a minimal counterexample.

substitutions.the absence of infinite descending chain: the ascending chain condition on ideals
substitutions.the minimal counterexample: an ideal maximal among those failing the property

validity_conditions: the ascending chain condition must hold, which is exactly what makes reverse inclusion well founded
the set of counterexample ideals must be nonempty for a maximal element to be extracted
the argument gives a maximal counterexample, not a maximum one, so uniqueness cannot be assumed
proof_plan: Suppose a property fails for some ideal, and let $\SS$ be the set of all ideals for which it fails.

By the [[Definition:Ascending Chain Condition|ascending chain condition]], the relation $I \prec J \iff I \supsetneq J$ has no infinite descending chains.
Hence $\prec$ is [[Definition:Well-Founded Relation|well-founded]].
By the minimal-counterexample principle, $\SS$ has a $\prec$-minimal element $I$, which is maximal under inclusion among the failures.

Every ideal strictly containing $I$ lies outside $\SS$, so satisfies the property.
Showing that the property lifts from all strictly larger ideals to $I$ gives a contradiction.

Hence $\SS = \O$, which is [[Principle of Noetherian Induction|Noetherian induction]].
{{qed}}
